meta.title: Worst headache of my life
learning_objectives: Take a headache history that distinguishes thunderclap from primary headache
De-escalate an angry patient while still gathering critical information
Recognise red flags for subarachnoid haemorrhage and other secondary headaches
references: Perry JJ et al. Clinical decision rules to rule out subarachnoid hemorrhage for acute headache. JAMA 2013 (Ottawa SAH Rule)

case.candidate_brief: You are an intern in the Emergency Department of a Brisbane hospital. Jess Thompson, 34, presented with a headache and was triaged as category 3. She has been waiting for 3 hours. Observations: HR 88, BP 158/94, RR 18, SpO2 99%, T 37.1°C, GCS 15. Take a history, then present your findings to the examiner.
case.assessment_task: Present your history, your differential diagnoses, and your immediate investigations and management.

patient.name: Jess Thompson
patient.background: Lives with her partner Sam in Brisbane's inner north.
patient.persona_notes: Frustrated, in pain and sensitive to light. Short, clipped answers at first; sarcastic about the wait ('Oh, NOW someone's here?'). Softens noticeably if the student apologises for the wait and takes her seriously. Becomes more upset if told it's 'probably just a migraine'.
patient.opening_statement: Finally. I've been sitting out there for three hours with the worst headache of my life and the triage nurse reckons it's a migraine. It's NOT a migraine.

presenting_complaint.site: Back of the head, now all over
presenting_complaint.onset: Sudden, while doing deadlifts at the gym about 6 hours ago; maximal within a minute
presenting_complaint.character: 'Like being hit in the back of the head with a cricket bat'
presenting_complaint.associated: Vomited twice, stiff neck, light hurts her eyes, briefly 'blacked out' at onset

facts.content: It's the worst headache I've ever had. Nothing like this, ever.
It came on in a split second, mid-deadlift. It was at its worst within a minute.
It started at the back of my head, like being whacked with a cricket bat. Now it's everywhere.
It was about six hours ago, around 9 this morning.
I've thrown up twice.
My neck is really stiff and sore.
The lights in here are killing me.
Sam said I sort of went blank and dropped the bar for a few seconds. I don't really remember.
No weakness or numbness. My vision's okay apart from the light hurting.
No fever that I know of, no rash, I wasn't sick before this.
I didn't hit my head on anything.
I get migraines a few times a year, but they build up slowly with flashing lights first. This is completely different.
I'm on the pill, the combined one. And sumatriptan for my migraines, but I haven't taken any today.
I had two Panadeine in the car on the way here. Didn't touch it.
No allergies.
My mum had a bleed on the brain when she was 50. She was in hospital for ages.
I smoke, about five a day. I know, I know.
Few drinks on the weekend. No drugs.
I keep thinking about what happened to Mum.
I'm scared something's burst in my head and nobody's taking me seriously.
I want a scan. I'm not leaving until someone actually checks.

ice.ideas: Something like her mother's 'bleed on the brain'
ice.expectations: A scan and to be taken seriously

behaviour_rules: Stays curt and sarcastic until the student acknowledges the wait and her distress
Becomes angrier if told it's probably a migraine or to 'calm down'
Asks the student to dim the lights or talk more quietly if they talk loudly
Once rapport is built, answers fully and admits she's scared

differentials.discriminating_features: Thunderclap onset during exertion, worst ever, neck stiffness, vomiting, brief LOC, family history of brain haemorrhage, smoker
Combined OCP and smoking are risk factors; usually subacute onset, may cause seizures or papilloedema
Recurrent thunderclap headaches, triggered by exertion or vasoactive drugs (e.g. triptans)
Neck pain after strain, may have focal neurology or Horner syndrome
Fever, rash, systemic illness. Absent here, and onset too abrupt
Diagnosis of exclusion. Her typical migraines are gradual with aura, so this differs from her usual pattern

red_flags.why: First or worst headache is a red flag for secondary causes
Thunderclap onset (peaks within 1 minute) mandates SAH work-up
Meningism suggests blood or infection in the subarachnoid space
Loss of consciousness at onset is part of the Ottawa SAH Rule
First-degree relative with likely aneurysmal haemorrhage increases risk

expected_investigations: Urgent non-contrast CT brain (highly sensitive within 6 hours of onset)
If CT is negative but suspicion remains: CT angiography and/or lumbar puncture for xanthochromia at least 12 hours after onset, per local pathway
FBC, UEC, coagulation profile, group and hold, glucose
expected_management: Re-triage and escalate immediately to the senior ED doctor; move to a monitored bed
Analgesia and antiemetic; keep nil by mouth
Neurosurgical referral if SAH is confirmed; BP management and nimodipine per specialist advice
Communicate honestly: acknowledge the wait, explain the plan and why it's urgent
safety_netting: Tell staff immediately if she gets drowsy, confused, weak, or the headache worsens
Do not discharge as a migraine without excluding SAH

examiner_question_bank.question: What is the Ottawa SAH Rule, and which of its criteria does she meet?
Her CT at 7 hours is reported as normal. What would you do next?
What features would make you consider cerebral venous sinus thrombosis?
How did you approach her frustration about the wait?

items.label: Establishes thunderclap onset: sudden, maximal within a minute, during exertion
Elicits neck stiffness, vomiting, brief loss of consciousness and photophobia
Screens for focal neurology, fever/rash and trauma
Takes a medication and allergy history, including the combined OCP and triptan use
Asks about family history and smoking
Acknowledges the wait and her frustration; de-escalates without being defensive
Explores her fear about her mother's history and her wish for a scan
Gives subarachnoid haemorrhage as the leading diagnosis
Considers CVST, dissection, RCVS and meningitis, with reasons
Requests an urgent non-contrast CT brain
Knows the next step if CT is negative (LP ≥12 h for xanthochromia and/or CTA)
Escalates to a senior, monitors neuro obs, gives analgesia/antiemetic, keeps nil by mouth
Recognises that this is not a migraine until proven otherwise and acts urgently
